extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and creative writers interested in myth, symbolism, and poetic description
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating mythic/poetic narratives and symbol-laden descriptive writing, especially treatments of Demeter/Persephone-type material connecting ritual, nature, and personification. Focuses on imagery, symbolic temper, and the relation of myth to ritual and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism as a special temper
rubrics_metrics.description: “Symbolism intense as this, is the creation of a special temper, in which a certain simplicity, taking all things literally, au pied de la lettre, is united to a vivid pre-occupation with the aesthetic beauty of the image itself, the figured side of figurative expression, the form of the metaphor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful symbolism combines literal simplicity with an intense focus on the aesthetic shape of the image; treat metaphors as formed, visible objects and attend to the 'figured' side of expression. Examples: Giotto's handling of Biblical images; the designer of the fourteenth-century Apocalypse window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification must avoid mere allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: “The personification of abstract ideas by modern painters or sculptors... shocks, in most cases, the aesthetic sense, as something conventional or rhetorical, as a mere transparent allegory.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving abstract ideas human form, aim for depth and sympathetic penetration so the figure feels more than a label. Contrast shallow, rhetorical personification with profound, poetical representations such as Giotto's Virtues and Vices, which are connected with an artist's sympathetic insight into the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to small, literal details in symbolic figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic representation "cares a great deal for the hair of Temperance, discreetly bound, for some subtler likeness to the colour of the sky in the girdle of Hope, for the inwoven flames in the red garment of Charity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, specific details (hair, colour, woven motifs) strengthen symbolic figures and make them convincing. Details should be chosen to reflect and deepen the symbolic meaning rather than serve as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical/age-appropriate temper
rubrics_metrics.description: “These fruits of individual genius are in part also a 'survival' from a different age, with the whole mood of which this mode of expression was more congruous than it is with ours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain modes of symbolism or personification suit particular historical moods. When adopting archaic or intense symbolic modes, acknowledge the age or temper that makes them feel natural; the quality may be a survival from earlier artistic sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mingling cosmical/mystical import with personal narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mingling of the primitive cosmical import of the myth with the later, personal interests of the story” (e.g., Homeric hymn turns natural year changes into a personal history of affection and sorrow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend the grand, cosmological elements of a myth with intimate human feeling to enrich meaning: let natural cycles personify grief, renewal, and other human experiences so that mythic and personal layers echo one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive passages should be picture-like and particular
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Homeric hymn is the central monument... the story lends itself naturally to description, and it is in descriptive beauties that the Homeric hymn excels; its episodes are finished designs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose descriptive episodes as finished images—use concrete nouns (flowers, wells, olive-trees), careful naming, and compositional unity to create scenes that could be painted. Weaving precise names and sensory detail strengthens the visual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect narrative incidents to ritual and custom
rubrics_metrics.description: “Many of its incidents are probably suggested by the circumstances and details of the Eleusinian ritual... religious usages before there were distinct religious conceptions, and these antecedent religious usages shape and determine, at many points, the ultimate religious conception.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground mythic narrative in ritual gestures, processions, and local observances; aligning story beats with ceremonial practices enhances authenticity and symbolic resonance (e.g., nine days of wandering ↔ nine days of festival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow myths to grow collectively and show local variations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story of Demeter... was the work of no single author or place or time; the poet of its first phase was no single person, but the whole consciousness of an age... The myth grew up gradually, and at many distant places, in many minds, independent of each other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or analyzing mythic material, value multiplicity and inconsistency as signs of organic growth; incorporate local epithets, incompatible incidents, and variant episodes rather than forcing uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sorrow/romantic spirit to extract beauty from difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: “The 'worship of sorrow'... the legend of Demeter and Persephone... is sufficient to show that the 'worship of sorrow' was not without its function in Greek religion; their legend is a legend made by and for sorrowful, wistful, anxious people... extracting by a kind of subtle alchemy, a beauty, not without the elements of tranquillity, of dignity and order, out of a matter, at first sight painful and strange.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy from themes of sorrow or difficulty; the Romantic temper can transform painful material into dignified, tranquil, and beautiful art. Evaluate how well a work converts tragic or strange subject-matter into aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification should produce 'real illusion' not rhetorical phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: “When it talked of the return of Kore to Demeter... was not using rhetorical language, but yielding to a real illusion; to which the voice of man 'was really a stream, beauty an effluence, death a mist.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful personification makes the illusion feel genuine and felt, not merely described. Language should yield sensory, lived metaphors that read as experienced reality rather than abstract commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about over-confident reconstruction from fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: “The student of origins... must be content to follow faint traces;... there is a certain cynicism too, in that over-positive temper, which is so jealous of our catching any resemblance in the earlier world to the thoughts that really occupy our own minds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative recreation or scholarly reconstruction of mythic origins, avoid asserting certainty from fragmentary evidence. Respect ambiguity and resist mapping modern conceptions onto ancient materials without allowance for doubt.
